analysis.one_liner: Speeds federal approval of mining projects on public land by capping reviews and limiting environmental study.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with two Republican cosponsors, never received a committee vote and died when the 115th Congress ended, leaving mine permitting rules unchanged.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced faster approval of hardrock mining projects on federal land. It capped the entire permitting review at 30 months, allowed a single agency to declare environmental review requirements met by its own written determination, and exempted mining in national forests from rules against cutting trees and building roads in roadless areas. It applied to mining applications already pending when it passed.
analysis.who_benefits: Mining companies with claims or projects on federal land gain the most: a 30-month cap on the whole review process, a single project lead coordinating agencies, a shortcut that deems environmental law satisfied when the lead agency signs off, freedom from national forest roadless restrictions, and the ability to put pending applications on the faster track [S2][S3]. Manufacturers that depend on imported minerals for defense and energy products could benefit indirectly if domestic supply expands [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hardrock mining companies on federal land

how_it_helps.text: Caps the total mine permitting review period at 30 months unless the company and the agency both agree to extend it, sharply limiting how long reviews can run.

Declares the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act satisfied if the lead agency determines, in a written decision, that factors like environmental impact and alternatives have been or will be addressed — reducing the full environmental review process to an agency determination.
Requires a single project lead to coordinate all agencies, set deadlines, and minimize delays, ending much of the back-and-forth between agencies that companies cite as a source of cost.
Exempts mining projects on national forest land from rules prohibiting tree cutting and road construction in unroaded areas, opening areas that were previously off-limits to road building.
Lets companies with applications already pending demand the faster process within 30 days of asking.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the cost: environmental review of mines on federal land would be shortened and partly replaced by the lead agency's own written determination, national forest roadless protections would be waived for mining, and taxpayers would rely on reclamation bonds set by the same agency that approved the mine to cover cleanup if a company walks away [S2][S3]. Communities near mines would have less time and a thinner record to challenge or shape projects.
analysis.who_pays_short: Public lands, nearby communities, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill lets the lead agency declare the core environmental review law satisfied through its own written rationale, weakening the independent analysis that currently examines a mine's impacts, alternatives, and irreversible resource losses before approval.

A 30-month ceiling on the entire review — including the environmental study, agency consultations, and public comment — can force rushed decisions on large mines whose water pollution and land damage last for decades.
Exempting national forest projects from roadless-area protections means new road construction and tree cutting in unroaded forest, with effects that extend beyond the mine itself.
It applies retroactively to applications already filed, changing the rules mid-process for projects the public was reviewing under the old standards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument on the other side: the U.S. imports most of many minerals used in defense and clean energy, and permitting delays of 7 to 10 years are cited as a top risk to domestic mining projects [S3]. Faster, better-coordinated permitting could serve national security and manufacturing. But the bill pursues that goal almost entirely by cutting corners — capping reviews at 30 months, letting one agency's memo substitute for full environmental study, and waiving forest roadless protections — rather than by adding staff or improving coordination while keeping scrutiny intact. For a process governing permanent, large-scale disturbance of public land, the design weighs speed over the public's ability to understand and shape what gets built.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dean Heller introduced the bill on January 12, 2017; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day.
Two Republican senators signed on as cosponsors, but the action history shows no hearing, no committee markup, and no floor vote ever occurred.
The bill sat in committee until the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, at which point it died and would have had to be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so the public kept the existing — slower but fuller — environmental review process for mines on federal land, and national forest roadless protections stayed in place. Mining companies that wanted faster permits got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public kept existing mine review rules

for.name: Dean Heller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

for.name: 2 of 52 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Democrat cosponsored.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup and never reported the bill; it died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only record of support is three Republican senators (the sponsor and two cosponsors), and the committee that buried it was itself chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: The bill would have cut permitting time and cost for companies extracting gold, copper, lithium, and other hardrock minerals from federal land — minerals they claim under an 1872-era law that charges no royalty — while shifting more of the environmental and cleanup risk to the public. Its 30-month cap, NEPA shortcut, and roadless exemption all reduce the scrutiny mines face.

industries.industry: Defense and clean-energy manufacturers dependent on imported minerals
industries.note: The bill's stated purpose is to expand domestic supply of minerals used in defense and energy technology, and faster domestic permitting could eventually ease their import dependence. But the bill only speeds approvals; it guarantees no new supply.

industries.industry: National forest recreation and tourism businesses
industries.note: By exempting mining from roadless-area protections on national forest land, the bill would have allowed new road construction and tree cutting in unroaded areas that recreation economies depend on.
